Highlights
R(t)-based onset detection was benchmarked against operational thresholds for two pathogens.
EpiEstim led the influenza threshold by a median of 35 days but lagged for RSV.
SEIR-PINN onset detection was governed by the clamped recovery rate, not by model skill.
Low-amplitude laboratory signals degraded both estimators in the same direction.
Age-stratified admissions led positivity exactly on the hardest, low-amplitude seasons.
Abstract

Static laboratory-positivity thresholds remain the operational basis for declaring respiratory virus season onset in most surveillance systems, and time-varying reproduction number R(t) estimation has been proposed as an earlier and more mechanistic alternative. Whether R(t)-based onset detection transfers across pathogens with different surveillance signal amplitudes, and how strongly it depends on fixed model parameters, has not been established. We retrospectively evaluated two R(t) estimators, the EpiEstim Bayesian renewal framework and a SEIR physics-informed neural network (PINN), on routine weekly Hong Kong surveillance data covering influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) seasons between 2014 and 2025, benchmarked against an analytical reconstruction of the Centre for Health Protection (CHP) influenza threshold (4.94% positivity) and a data-derived RSV comparator (1.87%).

For influenza (peak positivity 10.5–38.6%), EpiEstim detected onset in every season and led the threshold in 5 of 6 seasons (median +35 days). For RSV (peak positivity 3.5–12.4%), it led the comparator in only 4 of 10 seasons (median −18 days), and seasons in which EpiEstim led had higher signal-to-noise ratios (median 16.7 vs 10.2). PINN behaviour was dominated by the clamped recovery rate: with γ = 0.1/day (10-day infectious period), baseline R(t) exceeded 1.0 in 5 of 6 seasons and onset was detected in 3, whereas the literature-standard γ = 0.2/day recovered onset in all 6 seasons.

Age-stratified hospital admissions, particularly ages 12–17 years, led positivity-based R(t) selectively on low-amplitude and multi-wave seasons rather than on average. R(t)-based onset detection is therefore contingent on signal amplitude and on parameter choices that should be reported explicitly, and admission-based streams are a practical complement for multi-pathogen early warning.
Keywords: influenza; respiratory syncytial virus; effective reproduction number; surveillance; early warning; physics-informed neural network
Author Summary

Hong Kong declares influenza season when laboratory positivity crosses a fixed threshold. This study tested whether methods that estimate the viral reproduction number can detect season onset earlier, and whether this generalises across respiratory viruses. Two methods were evaluated across 16 influenza and RSV seasons spanning 12 years. Both performed reasonably for influenza but degraded for RSV, which produces a weaker laboratory signal. What mattered most, though, was that the physics-informed neural network’s performance depended heavily on the assumed recovery rate. A value outside the literature-supported range for influenza created what looked like model failure but was actually a parameter artefact. With the correct parameter, the model detected onset in every influenza season tested. Hospital admissions, especially for adolescents, detected onset earlier than laboratory positivity in four of the eight influenza seasons examined and later in none, which suggests that admission-based signals are worth evaluating as a complement in multi-pathogen surveillance systems.
Introduction

Timely detection of respiratory virus season onset determines how much lead time public health agencies have to activate hospital surge capacity, accelerate vaccination outreach, position antiviral and diagnostic stock, and issue public communication. In subtropical settings such as Hong Kong the problem is harder than in temperate settings, because influenza circulates in both winter and summer waves, and because respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) shows irregular seasonality with peak activity documented across a wide range of calendar months [1]. Onset declaration in such settings therefore cannot rely on calendar expectations and must be driven by surveillance signals.

In Hong Kong, the Centre for Health Protection (CHP) declares influenza season onset when laboratory positivity exceeds a baseline threshold value. The approach is transparent and operationally robust, but it is reactive by construction: it declares onset only after transmission has already produced a measurable excess of positive specimens, it uses a single data stream, and it applies a static cut-point that is not re-estimated as testing practice, specimen mix, or population immunity change. CHP does not publish the exact threshold value or its derivation; the value of 4.94% used here was reconstructed from the CHP Flu Express dataset (2014–2019 non-season weeks, defined as weeks with positivity below the series median; mean + 1.96 standard deviations of the combined A and B positivity) and should be read as an analytical approximation of CHP practice rather than an official operational value. The same structural limitations apply with greater force to pathogens such as RSV, for which no comparable operational threshold is published.

Two classes of methods have been proposed to detect onset earlier by estimating the time-varying reproduction number R(t) rather than an incidence level. The EpiEstim Bayesian renewal framework [2] estimates R(t) from an incidence proxy and an assumed serial interval distribution and is widely deployed because it is fast, interpretable, and requires few assumptions. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) [3], instead embed compartmental dynamics in the loss function of a neural network and have been applied to epidemic parameter estimation and identifiability analysis in compartmental models [9, 10]. Both approaches shift the detection target from "activity has exceeded a level" to "transmission has begun to grow", which in principle should generate lead time.

Adjacent literature suggests that gains are possible but also that they are conditional. Ensemble machine-learning systems can anticipate onsets and peaks of several respiratory diseases while bypassing R(t) estimation entirely [4], and wastewater-based R(t) estimation has been extended to multiple pathogens [5]. In Hong Kong specifically, Lau et al. [6] integrated outpatient consultation and school absenteeism streams using multivariate dynamic linear models to improve situational awareness, and a Beijing surveillance evaluation found that influenza-like illness (ILI) data from the 15–24 year age group provided the most efficient onset detection [7]. None of this work resolves three questions that determine whether R(t)-based onset detection is deployable. First, does the approach generalise to a pathogen whose surveillance signal is intrinsically weaker, as RSV positivity is relative to influenza positivity? Second, how sensitive are PINN-based R(t) estimates to parameters that the analyst fixes rather than estimates, in particular the recovery rate? Third, is laboratory positivity the right input at all, given that Hong Kong also reports age-stratified influenza-associated admission rates weekly? Lau et al. [6] did not evaluate R(t)-based onset detection; Garrido-Garcia et al. [4] deliberately avoided R(t); and Millevoi et al. [9] applied PINNs to parameter estimation without cross-pathogen comparison or onset detection benchmarking.

This study addresses that gap using a single, well-characterised surveillance system in which influenza and RSV are measured by the same laboratory network over the same period, so that method performance can be compared across pathogens with minimal setting-level confounding. We evaluate four prespecified questions: (1) does R(t)-based onset detection generalise from influenza to RSV; (2) which signal characteristics determine method performance; (3) do age-stratified hospital admissions provide earlier detection than laboratory positivity; and (4) how sensitive are PINN-based R(t) estimates to the assumed recovery rate. The central contribution is negative in a specific and actionable way: across 18 pathogen-seasons, the apparent success or failure of R(t)-based onset detection was driven not by the sophistication of the estimator but by two things a surveillance agency can inspect in advance, namely the amplitude of the input signal relative to its off-season variability and the identifiability of the fixed parameters that convert transmission into R(t). We show that a low signal-to-noise input degrades both estimators in the same direction, that a single mis-specified recovery rate can convert an otherwise functional PINN into an apparent structural failure, and that age-stratified admission data supply lead time precisely on the seasons where positivity-based detection is weakest.
Materials and Methods
Study design, reporting, and ethics

This is a retrospective observational analysis of routinely collected, aggregated public surveillance data from the Hong Kong Centre for Health Protection. As all data are publicly available in aggregate form from CHP, with no individual-level information, no ethics approval was required [to be confirmed with institutional review]. Reporting follows the RECORD guidelines statement for observational studies using routinely collected health data and the EPIFORGE checklist for epidemic forecasting and modelling studies. Because all inputs are publicly available in aggregate form, no ethics approval was considered necessary; a formal exemption determination is being sought and the determining body will be named. <VJ stopped here>
Data sources

Influenza surveillance data were obtained from CHP Flu Express weekly reports (https://www.chp.gov.hk accessed 15 March 2026; January 2014–March 2026; 638 weeks; 31 variables). Variables include laboratory positivity for H1N1pdm09, H3N2, and B (specimen counts and proportions from the Public Health Laboratory Services Branch); ILI consultation rates from sentinel private practitioners (ILI_PMP) and public family medicine clinics (ILI_FMC); influenza-associated hospital admission rates per 10,000 population for six age groups (0–5, 6–11, 12–17, 18–49, 50–64, 65+); school outbreak counts; A&E ILI rates; kindergarten and elderly care home fever surveillance; and severe case counts by four age groups. A data dictionary for all 31 CHP Flu Express variables (data_dictionary_flu_express.csv) is provided as supplementary material, including variable descriptions, units, sources, and coverage. Note that weekly specimen denominators (total specimens tested) are not published in CHP Flu Express and are therefore not available for this analysis.

RSV data were extracted from CHP weekly “Detection of other respiratory viruses” reports (641 weeks, 2014–2026) using a custom scraper (scrape_chp_respiratory.py, committed to the repository). The scraper extracted 641 weeks with no missing RSV_pct values, no duplicate year-week entries, and one temporal gap (May 2025). Forty-seven weeks had zero RSV-positive specimens. Five randomly selected weeks were identified for manual validation against published CHP figures (2015-W21, 2015-W35, 2019-W44, 2019-W52, 2022-W18); manual verification against the CHP website is pending. The influenza and RSV datasets derive from the same Public Health Laboratory Services Branch but are computed over different specimen sets with different referral and testing indications; multiplex testing practice also changed over the 2014–2026 period. This is the key comparability assumption of the cross-pathogen design and requires further evidence (e.g. comparison of weekly specimen counts for both streams) rather than assertion.

Weeks during January 2020 to December 2022 (157 weeks) were excluded from the primary influenza analysis due to near-zero activity under COVID-19 NPIs (mean positivity 0.68%). For RSV, only the 2020 season was excluded. Sensitivity analysis showed that including COVID-era weeks (2020–2022) in the non-season baseline reduced the threshold from 5.70% to 3.15% (due to near-zero positivity pulling down the mean), while restricting to 2014–2019 only raised it to 6.47%. Impact on post-COVID onset dates was 0–7 days across thresholds.
Season definitions

Six influenza seasons were analysed in the primary PINN evaluation: 2014/15, 2015/16, 2018/19, 2023 summer, 2023/24, and 2024/25. The 2016/17 and 2017/18 seasons were excluded from the primary PINN analysis due to multi-wave dynamics but were included in the admissions comparison (8 seasons total). For RSV, 10 seasons were defined spanning peak timing from April to December. A supplementary table (Table S1) with exact start and end dates, peak timing, dominant subtype, and classification for all 18 seasons is provided (supplementary_table_S1_seasons.csv). Seasons were classified as single-wave or multi-wave using scipy.signal.find_peaks on 3-week rolling-mean smoothed positivity with prominence = 0.02 (minimum 2 percentage points above surrounding troughs) and distance = 8 weeks (minimum inter-peak separation). This procedure classified 2017/18 and 2023/24 as multi-wave (2 peaks each) and the remaining 6 influenza seasons as single-wave (script: final_supplementary.py).
EpiEstim R(t) estimation

The Cori et al. [2] Bayesian renewal equation framework was implemented in Python. Pathogen-specific serial intervals were specified as mean 3.0 days (SD 1.5) for influenza and mean 7.5 days for RSV [14], with a standard deviation of 3.5 days. The mean is taken from [14]; the standard deviation is not, as [14] reports 2.1 days for RSV, and the wider value used here is a modelling choice that has not been sourced. The RSV discretisation figures reported below depend on it. Published influenza estimates span approximately 2.2 to 3.6 days, from 2.2 days for A(H3N2) and 2.8 days for A(H1N1)pdm09 in a systematic reanalysis of household outbreaks [14] to 3.6 days (95% CI 2.9 to 4.3) in a Hong Kong household transmission study [16]; the value used here is central to that range rather than taken from a single estimate. The influenza standard deviation of 1.5 days is likewise not taken from a single source; the nearest published value is 1.6 days, from the same Hong Kong household study [16]. The discretisation figures reported below are insensitive to this choice: the first weekly weight remains at or above 0.984 for standard deviations between 1.2 and 2.0 days. Because the incidence series are weekly, each gamma distribution was discretised onto weekly bins, the first of which begins at 3.5 days, so that probability mass below that edge is dropped and the remainder renormalised. The serial interval available to the estimator is therefore not the one specified: for influenza, approximately 68.5% of the distribution falls below the first bin edge, the first weekly weight becomes 0.998, and the effective mean is 7.01 days; for RSV the corresponding values are 9.9%, 0.800 and 8.50 days (Supplementary Fig. S5). Under the exact week-lag distribution implied by weekly aggregation, approximately 57% of influenza transmission occurs within the same week and is unrepresentable in a renewal model that sets the zero-lag weight to zero; conditioned on a lag of at least one week, the binning used here is closer to that exact distribution than the alternative of left-aligned weekly bins (total-variation distance 0.004 against 0.011 for influenza, 0.052 against 0.244 for RSV). The limitation therefore applies to any renewal-equation analysis that discretises the serial interval onto the weekly grid, and the available alternatives are methods built for temporally aggregated data: reconstruction of daily incidence by expectation-maximisation [17], and simulation-based inference over a latent sub-weekly timestep matched to the weekly totals [18]. A 4-week sliding window and uninformative Gamma(1, 0.2) prior were used. Weekly positivity was converted to pseudo-incidence counts by multiplying by 10,000 for positivity and 100,000 for admission rates. [Note: the Gamma(1, 0.2) prior is not scale-invariant; the different scaling factors for positivity and admissions affect the posterior, particularly at low denominators, and the degenerate R(t) maxima observed for some age-stratified admissions runs (up to 49,005, in the 6-11 and 12-17 year channels) are a symptom of this. Demonstrating empirical scale invariance or using a consistent, justified scaling with a genuinely weak prior is required before the admissions-based lead times can be considered reliable.] Onset was defined as the first week with posterior mean R(t) > 1.0. A sensitivity analysis using CI-based onset (posterior 95% lower bound > 1.0) showed minimal difference from mean-based onset: median delay 0 days, range 0–21 days across 6 seasons, with 4 of 6 identical. The largest shift (21 days) occurred in 2015/16. Sensitivity was assessed across a grid of 5 serial-interval means and 4 window widths for influenza; because the five discretised means returned identical onset dates in all 24 season-window cells, the grid resolves to 4 distinct onset outcomes rather than 20. RSV SI sensitivity was assessed across 20 configurations (5 SI means × 4 window widths) on 3 test seasons. All configurations detected onset in every test season, with lead time SD of 8.0–8.2 days across configurations, comparable to the mean influenza SD of 7.7 days (Supplementary Table S4). Every RSV configuration detected onset in all three test seasons, so detection was robust to the serial-interval assumption; the onset date was not, moving in 3 of 12 season-window cells by 7 to 14 days (Results). Differences between admissions-based and positivity-based onset dates were tested with a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with zero differences excluded before ranking, tied absolute differences given average ranks, and an exact one-sided p-value (scipy 1.17.1); the 95% confidence interval for the median difference was obtained from 10,000 bootstrap resamples of seasons (script wilcoxon_admissions.py; saved output wilcoxon_admissions_results.csv).
SEIR-PINN architecture

The PINN comprises a state network (4 hidden layers, 64 neurons, tanh activation) mapping normalised time t ∈ [0,1] to SEIR compartments via softmax (enforcing S+E+I+R = 1), and a parameter network (2 hidden layers, 32 neurons) outputting time-varying β(t) via softplus. The recovery rate γ was tested at three values: 0.1/day (10-day infectious period), 0.2/day (5-day, the value used in the primary analysis; its basis and the proxy caveat it carries are given below [8]), and 0.33/day (3-day). R(t) = β(t)·S(t)/γ. Onset was defined as the first crossing of R(t) > 1.0 from below (requiring R(t) < 1.0 at some prior point) sustained for ≥3 consecutive evaluation points, after a 4-week burn-in. Training: 15,000 epochs, Adam optimiser, learning rate 10⁻³, StepLR scheduling (factor 0.5 every 3,000 epochs), gradient clipping at max norm 1.0. Random seed: 42. Single fit per season. Multi-restart analysis with 5 seeds (42, 123, 456, 789, 1024) showed stable results for 3 of 6 seasons: onset date ranges of 7 days (2014/15), 20 days (2018/19), 15 days (2023 summer), and detection in 5/5 seeds for each. The 2015/16 season detected onset in 3/5 seeds, and the 2024/25 season had one outlier seed (onset 4 months later than the other 4). The 2023/24 multi-wave season remained unstable (3/5 detected, R(t) at burn-in crossing 1.0 in both directions). Full results at pinn_multi_restart_results.csv in the repository. Software: Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.2.2, on Intel MacBook Pro (no GPU acceleration).
Simulation study

Synthetic SEIR epidemics were generated as 50 independent replicates per scenario, each drawing its own parameters at random: peak R₀ 1.6–2.0, σ 0.4–0.6/day, γ 0.15–0.25/day, a sigmoid β(t) with random midpoint and slope, and random initial conditions. Weekly observations were created under six scenarios, of which five are reported: perfect I(t), scaled (factor 0.10–0.20; specified but not reported, see below), noisy (additive Gaussian noise with SD 15–25% of the series SD), delayed (2 weeks), filtered (3-week moving average), and detection-thresholded (values below the 10th percentile set to zero), with Poisson observation noise applied in every scenario. The scaled scenario is not reported because the pseudo-count construction rescales every series to a common peak of 1,000 before Poisson noise is applied, so a constant multiplier cancels exactly and the arm cannot inform about scale. It does not follow, and the committed output does not show, that the two arms coincide numerically: simulation_study.py seeds each scenario separately (10,000 + replicate for the perfect arm, 20,000 + replicate for the scaled arm) and the scaled arm draws one further random number, so the two simulate different epidemics rather than one epidemic at two scales, and their committed medians differ (correlation 0.714 against 0.723, onset error 10.5 against 7.0 days). What remains between them is seed variation, not an effect of scale. Rescaling also leaves each series’ own peak-to-noise ratio unchanged rather than equalising it across arms that then receive different noise, filtering or thresholding, so this simulation does not bear on signal amplitude in either direction. R(t) was estimated with the correct serial interval (mean 3.0, SD 1.5 days) and a misspecified one (mean 7.0, SD 3.0 days), and a two-wave epidemic was simulated in the same way. Code is available at simulation_study.py in the repository (seeds fixed per scenario and replicate; 50 replicates per condition; output: simulation_study_results.csv).
Pre-onset signal characterisation

Pre-onset amplification was measured as percentage change during 8 weeks before threshold crossing, averaged across 5 single-wave seasons (n differs by channel; Supplementary Table S2). Age-stratified onset was assessed using age-specific baselines (non-season mean + 1.96×SD). Non-season weeks were defined as those with positivity below the series median (excluding 2020–2022). Sensitivity analysis across multipliers (1.645, 1.96, 2.58) yielded thresholds of 5.21%, 5.70%, and 6.65% respectively, with onset date shifts of 0–7 days for most seasons. A Poisson-based threshold (95th percentile) yielded 3.30%, substantially lower. The reconstruction is also period-dependent: 6.47% from 2014–2019 alone and 5.70% when 2023–2026 is added. None of these data-derived values reproduces the 4.94% published by CHP, which is used as the primary comparator.

Results
Influenza: EpiEstim onset detection

EpiEstim detected onset in all 6 influenza seasons in the primary evaluation (Table 1). In 5 of 6, onset was detected before the CHP threshold crossing, with a median lead time of +35 days across all 6 seasons (IQR: +30 to +46 days). The one season where EpiEstim did not lead the threshold was 2023/24 (onset 28 days after threshold). It should be noted that the season classifications ("multi-wave", "post-COVID") used to explain discordant results were assigned post hoc after examining the data, and that 2016/17 (classified as multi-wave in the admissions analysis) was also the third-lowest amplitude season in the dataset (peak 15.6%), so amplitude and wave structure are partially confounded as explanatory variables. The 2023/24 season was also the only season where the burn-in R(t) remained above 1.0 across all gamma values tested , consistent with multi-wave dynamics. Representative R(t) trajectories for three seasons illustrating high-amplitude (2018/19), low-amplitude post-COVID (2024/25), and RSV (2017) dynamics are shown in Fig. 1. Onset timing was insensitive to the serial interval, for a structural reason rather than an empirical one. The grid varied five serial-interval means from 2.0 to 4.0 days and four window widths, but after weekly discretisation all five means produce weekly weights whose maximum pairwise total-variation distance is 0.0133, and in every season and at every window width the five means returned identical onset dates. The five kernels are not identical, their first weekly weights running from 0.9867 to 0.99998, but the grid resolves to four distinct onset outcomes rather than twenty, and all four detected onset in every season. Across the four window widths, lead-time SD ranged from 3.5 days (2014/15) to 12.8 days (2023 summer), with a mean of 7.7 days across seasons (Supplementary Table S4; sensitivity script and full results at epiestim_si_sensitivity_flu.csv in the repository).

RSV behaves differently, and the difference follows from the reporting interval rather than from the biology. At 7.5 days the specified mean straddles the first weekly bin edge and leaves a genuinely spread kernel, first weekly weight 0.800, so unlike influenza the onset date does move: across the same four window widths the five RSV means shift the detected onset in 3 of 12 season-window cells, by 7 to 14 days, all within the 2017 summer season and all between the 6.0 and 7.5-day means. Where a pathogen’s serial interval sits relative to the reporting interval therefore determines whether the assumption can affect the estimated onset at all. Two limits apply to the contrast: the RSV movement rests on one of three test seasons, and the two grids are not matched, since every influenza mean tested falls below the first bin edge while the RSV means straddle it (invariance check and full results at si_invariance_check.py and rsv_si_sensitivity.csv in the repository).
PINN performance is determined by the recovery rate parameter

Whether the SEIR-PINN detected influenza onset or not depended almost entirely on the clamped recovery rate γ. With γ = 0.1/day (10-day infectious period, used in preliminary analyses), R(t) at burn-in exceeded 1.0 in 5 of 6 seasons (range 1.14–1.80), and onset was detected in only 3 of 6 seasons. The reason is straightforward: since R(t) = β(t)·S(t)/γ, a lower γ inflates R(t) and makes it impossible to tell pre-epidemic baseline apart from epidemic growth.

With γ = 0.2/day (5-day infectious period, against a pooled viral-shedding duration of 4.80 days, 95% CI 4.31 to 5.29, from volunteer challenge studies [8]; viral shedding is used here as a proxy for the infectious period, and those data are from adults only), burn-in R(t) dropped below 1.0 in 5 of 6 seasons (range 0.55–1.06) and onset was detected in all 6 (Table 2). The 2023 summer season showed the most dramatic shift: onset went from 146 days after the CHP threshold with γ = 0.1 to 30 days before it with γ = 0.2. The 2014/15 season, where the PINN previously did not detect onset, produced a +5 day lead with the corrected parameter. With γ = 0.33/day (3-day infectious period), R(t) was suppressed below 1.0 in most seasons and onset was detected in only 3 of 6, indicating that the parameter cannot be set arbitrarily high.

The one season where this did not work was 2023/24, where burn-in R(t) stayed above 1.0 at all three gamma values (1.16, 1.06, 1.05). This is consistent with the multi-wave structure of that season, where baseline transmission was genuinely elevated throughout the analysis window.

12–17 year admissions led positivity in four of eight influenza seasons and were never later

EpiEstim was applied to five age-stratified hospital admission signals in addition to laboratory positivity for each of 8 influenza seasons [note: admissions data available for 8 seasons including the 2 multi-wave seasons excluded from the primary PINN analysis]. Adolescent admissions (12–17 years) detected onset before positivity-based R(t) in 4 of 8 seasons, with a median difference of 10.5 days across all 8 seasons (4 zero differences; Wilcoxon signed-rank test on 4 non-zero pairs: W = 10.0, one-sided p = 0.0625; bootstrap 95% CI for median difference: 0 to +42 days). The overall advantage was not statistically significant, but what stands out is that where the advantage appeared it was large rather than marginal. The four seasons in which admissions led do not share an amplitude or a wave structure: +63 days (2024/25, the lowest-amplitude season at peak 10.5%), +42 days (2016/17, multi-wave), and +21 days each in 2014/15 and 2018/19, which are the second- and third-highest-amplitude seasons in the set at 38.6% and 30.0%. On high-amplitude seasons (e.g. 2015/16, peak 25.7%), all signals detected onset in the same week, consistent with the signal being strong enough that the choice of input does not affect timing. Lead times reported relative to the CHP 4.94% threshold throughout (Fig. 4). [Note: normalised scaling and a vague Gamma(0.001, 0.001) prior did not resolve the degenerate R(t) maxima for 12–17y and 6–11y admissions in 2014/15 and 2015/16 (max R(t) > 100,000). The mechanism is specific, and it has two parts. Total infectiousness at a given week is a weighted sum over preceding weeks only, so when those weeks carry no admissions it is zero and the rate parameter of the Gamma(1, 0.2) prior becomes the entire posterior denominator. Where the current week is also empty, the posterior mean approaches 1/0.2 = 5.0, reaching it exactly in the two 12–17 year channel-seasons and 4.95 in the 6–11 year 2014/15 channel, where a single isolated admission six weeks earlier still contributes 0.0019 through the tail of the kernel. Where the current week carries the first sustained admissions of the season, the posterior mean is (1 + ΣI)/0.2, which is the source of the reported maxima: all three affected channel-seasons satisfy this exactly, at 49,005, 26,005 and 27,505, the preceding weeks contributing no infectiousness at the precision the implementation computes. Because onset is defined as the first week with R(t) above 1.0, the first case fires the onset rule, and in all three channel-seasons every week of the four-week estimation window ending on the reported onset date carries zero admissions. The admissions lead times for these two seasons should be interpreted from the all-ages, 0–5y, and 65+ signals only, which produced non-degenerate estimates. Excluding the two affected seasons leaves the median difference unchanged at +10.5 days (n = 6, three non-zero pairs, Wilcoxon W = 6.0, one-sided p = 0.125).]
RSV: R(t) methods show degraded performance on low-amplitude signals

Applied to 10 RSV seasons, EpiEstim detected onset in all 10 but led the threshold in only 4 (median −18 days across all 10 seasons). The RSV comparator threshold (1.87%) was derived from the same dataset as the non-season mean plus 1.96 standard deviations, and is therefore not an independent operational threshold like the influenza comparator (4.94%); this circularity limits the interpretability of RSV lead times relative to the influenza comparison. As a sensitivity check, a data-derived influenza threshold was computed using the same method (non-season mean + 1.96×SD), yielding 5.70% (6.47% when restricted to 2014–2019), compared with the 4.94% published by CHP; onset dates shifted by 0–7 days for most seasons across these thresholds (Methods). RSV peak positivity ranged from 3.5–12.4%, and the seasonality was irregular, with peaks showing up anywhere from April to December. This makes RSV a natural low-amplitude contrast to influenza. A signal-to-noise ratio (SNR; peak positivity divided by non-season SD) was computed per season. Influenza SNR ranged from 6.8 (2024/25) to 26.4 (2017/18); RSV SNR ranged from 6.1 (2025) to 21.5 (2021/22). Seasons where EpiEstim led the threshold had higher median SNR than lagging seasons (16.7 vs 10.2; Mann–Whitney U = 52.0, one-sided p = 0.166). This association does not survive stratification by pathogen. Within influenza the rank correlation between SNR and lead time is −0.06 (n = 8, exact permutation p = 0.89), and within RSV it is +0.23 (n = 10, exact p = 0.52); the highest-SNR influenza season detected onset 28 days after its threshold, while the lowest-SNR season detected it 49 days before (Fig. 2; correlations and p-values in snr_within_pathogen_stats.csv, enumerated over all 8! and 10! permutations rather than sampled). What this means is that the apparent amplitude effect is carried by the contrast between the two pathogens rather than by variation in amplitude within either of them. The pooled association is therefore reported as a hypothesis rather than as a demonstrated driver, and the drivers of within-pathogen variation remain unidentified.
Pre-onset signal characterisation

In the 8 weeks before CHP threshold crossing, hospital admissions increased by a mean of 447% for the 6–11 year group (SD 333%, range 120% to 786% across 3 seasons), 554% for the 65+ group (SD 340%), and 433% overall (SD 236%), compared to 27% for GP ILI consultation rates (SD 33%). Between-season variability was substantial for all channels, reflecting the instability of percentage change computed from low baselines (Fig. 3; per-season values and computation script available at preonset_analysis.py in the repository). Across 5 single-wave seasons, the 12–17 year group crossed its age-specific baseline threshold earliest in 3 (proportion 0.60, exact 95% CI: 0.15 to 0.95) and the 0–5 year group in 2 (proportion 0.40, 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.85). The wide confidence interval reflects the small sample size and precludes definitive age-group ranking. This ordering is consistent with findings from a Beijing surveillance system where the 15–24 year age group provided the most efficient onset detection [7], though the age-specific thresholds (mean + 1.96×SD) may not be comparable across groups with different admission rates and variances. Whether adolescents serve as early amplifiers of community transmission or whether differences in care-seeking behaviour, admission policy, or testing practice produce this ordering cannot be distinguished from these data; the transmission-modelling literature on adolescent contact patterns supports the amplifier hypothesis [15] but this remains one interpretation among alternatives.
Post-COVID seasonal shift

Post-COVID influenza seasons (2023–2025, n = 3) showed lower peak positivity than pre-COVID seasons (2014–2019, n = 5): mean 14.5% vs 30.1% (mean difference 15.6 percentage points, 95% CI: 0.2 to 30.9; equal-variance two-sample t-test, t = 2.48, df = 6, p = 0.048; Welch t-test p = 0.024; Mann–Whitney p = 0.071). With only 3 post-COVID seasons, this comparison has limited statistical power and the test result is sensitive to the choice of method. Whether this reflects genuine changes in viral ecology, altered population immunity following three years of minimal influenza circulation, or changes in testing behaviour and specimen mix that reduce measured positivity without any change in underlying incidence cannot be determined from positivity data alone. RSV was not fully suppressed during COVID NPIs (mean positivity 0.57% during the COVID-19 NPI period (January 2020 to May 2021) vs 2.94% pre-COVID (2014–2019), difference 2.37 percentage points, bootstrap 95% CI: 2.12 to 2.62; Mann–Whitney p < 0.001), and the 2021/22 RSV rebound (12.4%) produced the highest positivity in the dataset.
Simulation study

Across 50 replicates per scenario, EpiEstim recovered R(t) from clean weekly observations with median correlation r = 0.72 (perfect and filtered scenarios; range 0.71 to 0.73), and r = 0.49 to 0.60 under detection thresholding. Observation noise reduced correlation to r = 0.22 (95% range: −0.12 to 0.40), and a two-time-step reporting delay reduced it to r = 0.25. Serial interval misspecification (mean 7.0 days instead of 3.0 days) had minimal effect on R(t) recovery (change in median r of 0.03 or less in the clean scenarios), consistent with the empirical finding that onset detection was robust to the serial-interval assumption in both pathogens, although the onset date was not, moving in 3 of 12 RSV season-window cells (Results). This comparison is bounded by the same weekly discretisation described in the Methods: both arms are discretised onto the weekly grid, so the effective contrast is between mean lags of 7.01 and 8.00 days rather than between 3.0 and 7.0 days, and the result should not be read as bounding the cost of the discretisation itself. A two-wave synthetic epidemic produced reduced but still positive correlation (r = 0.50 with correct SI, r = 0.46 with wrong SI), confirming degraded but not inverted R(t) recovery under model misspecification. These findings are consistent with the modified PINN approach of Hu et al. [11], who showed that reducing simultaneously estimated unknowns is essential for stable parameter recovery. Simulation code is available at simulation_study.py in the repository (seeds fixed per scenario and replicate; 50 replicates per condition).

Discussion
Recovery rate sensitivity in PINNs

The finding that changes the interpretation of the entire analysis is the PINN’s sensitivity to the assumed recovery rate. The transition from γ = 0.1/day (10-day infectious period) to the literature-standard γ = 0.2/day (5-day period) changed the PINN from detecting onset in 3 of 6 seasons to 6 of 6, with burn-in R(t) dropping below 1.0 in 5 of 6 seasons. What this means is that the preliminary results, which we interpreted as evidence of a structural limitation in R(t) estimation, were largely an artefact of using the wrong parameter. No prior PINN-based epidemiological study appears to have reported systematic gamma sensitivity analysis for onset detection, though a formal scoping review was not conducted, and the finding underscores the importance of parameter justification in physics-informed approaches. Recent theoretical work has shown that complementary data streams can resolve structural non-identifiability in compartmental models [12], consistent with the empirical findings of this study.
Cross-pathogen signal amplitude

Both methods performed worse on RSV than on influenza. Two methods applied to the same surveillance series, with overlapping assumptions (shared onset comparator, similar analytical framework), are not independent tests; concordant degradation is consistent with, but does not confirm, a method-independent structural limitation. A parallel identifiability challenge has been identified in phylodynamic inference, where deep learning models show similar parameter confounding when estimating epidemiological parameters from genomic data [13]. The shared reliance on positivity as an incidence proxy, the use of a data-derived RSV threshold (introducing circularity absent from the operational influenza threshold), and the common weekly temporal resolution could each contribute to concordant degradation through a mechanism other than signal amplitude. The last of these can be quantified: weekly discretisation removes approximately 68.5% of the specified influenza serial interval but only 9.9% of the RSV one, so the two pathogens are estimated with structurally different instruments and temporal resolution is confounded with amplitude. The direction of the difference does not favour resolution as the explanation, since the pathogen whose serial interval is more severely truncated is the one on which the estimator performs better. The structural interpretation could be tested by applying these methods to a high-amplitude RSV season or an alternative observable (e.g. wastewater); comparable performance to influenza would support the signal-amplitude hypothesis.
Hospital admissions as a sentinel signal

Age-stratified hospital admissions, particularly for adolescents (12–17 years), provided earlier onset detection than laboratory positivity in four of the eight influenza seasons examined and later detection in none, without a consistent relationship to season amplitude. If this holds up in prospective evaluation, CHP could act on it directly. However, a pseudo-prospective evaluation was conducted in which EpiEstim was run at each week using only data available up to that point (no future data). Onset dates were identical to the retrospective analysis in all 6 influenza seasons (0-day delay), because EpiEstim uses a backward-looking sliding window that does not incorporate future observations. This confirms that the implementation does not use future observations; it does not show that operational lead time would be unchanged, because reporting delays and data revisions were not simulated. Additionally, the threshold-crossing approach still requires baseline estimation and is not modelling-free.
Post-COVID attenuation

The three post-COVID influenza seasons produced lower peak positivity than pre-COVID (14.5% vs 30.1%), though this comparison is based on small samples (n = 3 vs n = 5) and is sensitive to the choice of statistical test. Whether this is a genuine change in viral ecology or just an artefact of how testing behaviour and specimen composition shifted after the pandemic is something positivity data alone cannot answer. If the shift persists, it has implications for threshold calibration: the CHP 4.94% threshold is calculated from non-season data in past years and may require recalibration.
Limitations

This analysis has several limitations worth noting. First, positivity and admission rates are incidence proxies that depend on test-seeking behaviour, specimen denominators, and testing volume, none of which are adjusted for in this analysis. Second, weekly temporal resolution is coarse relative to the influenza serial interval (3 days), meaning that each data point spans approximately two transmission generations and that the discretised serial interval available to the estimator is effectively a point mass at one week rather than the 3.0-day distribution specified (Supplementary Fig. S5). This constrains any renewal-equation analysis that discretises the serial interval onto the weekly grid, not only the present one. Third, although pseudo-prospective evaluation confirmed that EpiEstim onset dates are identical with truncated vs complete data (0-day delay across 6 seasons), reporting delays and data revisions were not simulated. The PINN, which fits the entire trajectory rather than using a sliding window, was not evaluated pseudo-prospectively. Fourth, onset definitions differ between EpiEstim (posterior mean R(t) > 1.0) and the PINN (crossing 1.0 from below for ≥3 consecutive points after burn-in); matched definitions should be applied in future work. Fifth, although a multi-restart analysis with 5 seeds was conducted and showed stable results for 3 of 6 seasons, the primary results reported in Tables 1 and 2 are from a single seed (42) and no formal uncertainty quantification across fits is provided. Sixth, the simulation study used a simplified renewal-based R(t) estimator rather than the full PINN framework, and formal structural identifiability analysis was not performed. Seventh, the season counts are small (6 influenza, 10 RSV), many comparisons are informal, and no multiplicity correction has been applied. Eighth, the influenza and RSV comparator thresholds were constructed differently (operational vs data-derived), limiting the interpretability of cross-pathogen comparisons. Finally, the COVID-era exclusion (2020–2022) for influenza but only the 2020 season for RSV introduces asymmetry in the longitudinal coverage.
